readerTitle: Revenue is up 60%. Should you still change direction?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 과외 서비스, 물리치료사용 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 'pivot or persevere' 회의 개념은 Eric Ries의 The Lean Startup에서 인용
insight: 방향 전환 시점은 매출 총액이 아니라, 여러 번의 진지한 시도가 핵심 숫자를 움직였는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 매출이 늘고 있으면 방향은 맞다. 일이 잘 안 풀린다고 느낄 때가 바꿀 때다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business. (정기적인 'pivot or persevere' 회의와 사전 기준 설정)

factChecks.note: Eric Ries가 The Lean Startup에서 정기적인 'pivot or persevere' 회의를 권한다는 내용을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적인 표현으로만 적었고 직접 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다.
물리치료 앱 수치(월 가입 약 40곳, 3개월 유지율 20% → 55%)와 과외 서비스 재등록률 70%는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Revenue is up 60%. Should you still change direction?
body: Maya runs a home cleaning service. In six months, monthly revenue went from $8,000 to $13,000.
Her friends say congratulations. But one number on her spreadsheet hasn't moved at all, and it may matter more than the total.

image.label: Rising revenue line next to a flat line
image.brief: 청소 도구(양동이, 걸레)가 놓인 책상 위 노트북 화면. 화면에 위로 올라가는 초록 선('Revenue')과 바닥에 평평하게 누운 회색 선('Customers who book again')이 나란히 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Growing, but customers don't come back.
body: Only about 18% of Maya's first-time home customers book a second clean. She tried three fixes: a repeat discount, a better checklist and reminder texts. The rate stayed between 17% and 19%.
Meanwhile, 12 small dental and medical offices hired her. Ten still book every week. What should she do?

options.text: Keep going. Revenue is growing, so the plan works
options.feedback: Growth feels safe, but she is replacing lost customers with new ones she pays to find. That gets more expensive, not less.

options.text: Try a fourth fix for homes, like a loyalty card
options.feedback: Testing more is reasonable, but three real tries already failed to move the number. A fourth small tweak likely buys time, not answers.

options.text: Shift focus to clinics, keeping home jobs that already pay
options.feedback: She follows the customers who pull hardest while keeping cash coming in. The cost is rebuilding sales and pricing for a new type of customer.

cards.title: What the total was hiding.
body: The total went up because ad spend tripled. Each month, she filled the same leaky bucket faster. The one group that stayed was one she never planned for.

cards.title: When to pivot
body: A **pivot** is changing one core part of your plan, such as who you serve or what problem you solve, while keeping what you've learned.
The time to pivot isn't when things feel hard. It's when **several real tries stop moving the number that matters most**, like how many customers come back.
Totals can rise while that number stays flat. Maya's did.

image.label: Three test arrows hitting a flat line
image.brief: 평평한 수평선 위로 세 개의 화살표('Discount', 'Checklist', 'Reminders')가 쏘아 올려지지만 모두 같은 높이에서 멈춤. 옆에 다른 방향으로 솟은 작은 막대('Clinics'). 깔끔한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Three signals, and a rule set in advance.
list: **The core number is flat** after several real experiments, not just one
**Growth only comes from spending more**, so you are buying it
**A pocket of customers pulls harder** than the market you planned for
cards.callout: Eric Ries, in *The Lean Startup*, suggests holding regular "pivot or persevere" meetings. Better still, write the rule before you start: "If repeat bookings aren't above 30% after three tests by June, we change direction."

cards.title: Slow totals can mean persevere.
body: Now picture a tutoring service. New families trickle in, and the owner feels stuck.
But 70% of families sign up again each term, and that share keeps rising. The product works. The problem is reach: too few people know about it.
Changing the service here would throw away the one thing that's working. The fix is marketing, not a pivot. Same feeling of being stuck, opposite answer.

image.label: Few arrivals, most staying
image.brief: 작은 교실 문으로 학생 몇 명만 들어오지만, 안에 있는 학생 대부분이 다음 학기 달력에 체크하는 모습. 따뜻한 색감의 플랫 일러스트. 실제 학원 상호 없음.

cards.title: Pivoting too early is also a mistake.
body: Each test needs enough customers and time to read. Ten customers in two weeks can tell you almost anything.
Every pivot also has costs. You may lose current customers, confuse staff and start learning from zero. Founders who pivot every few months never stay long enough to find out what works.
And check that the promising pocket is big enough to build a business on, not just loyal.

cards.title: Now it's an app for physiotherapists.
body: Your app lets physiotherapists send exercise plans to patients. Sign-ups have been flat at about 40 clinics a month for six months.
But after two onboarding changes, the share of clinics still active after three months rose from 20% to 55%. Your co-founder wants to switch to fitness coaches. What do you do?

options.text: Pivot to fitness coaches. Flat sign-ups mean the market is wrong
options.feedback: You'd abandon the one number that's clearly improving. Flat sign-ups point to a reach problem, not a product problem.

options.text: Persevere and put effort into reaching more clinics
options.feedback: Your tries are moving retention, the number that matters. The trade-off is patience: growth may stay slow while you fix how clinics find you.

options.text: Keep the clinics and build a coach version on the side
options.feedback: It hedges your bets, but splits a small team's attention just as the main product starts working.

cards.title: Pivot when your tries stop moving the number that matters.
body: Not when totals feel bad, and not when they look good. Watch the core number, give each test a fair chance, and follow the customers who pull hardest.
**Try it today:** write down your most important number, the target it must hit, and the date you'll change direction if it doesn't.
